claim: Childhood immunisation services have been disrupted by the COVID-19 pandemic in at least 68 countries during 2020 with around 80 million under 1-year-old children being affected.
source: Childhood immunisation services have been disrupted by the COVID-19 pandemic in at least 68 countries during 2020 with around 80 million under 1-year-old children being affected (Nelson, 2020; Science (AAAS), 2020; UNICEF, 2020; WHO, 2020a).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to external sources documenting the disruption statistics.

claim: Disruption to immunisation services occurred due to diversion of health care staff, facilities, and finances to deal with COVID-19 treatment and response.
source: This has occurred for several reasons – the diversion of health care staff, facilities, and finances to deal with COVID-19 treatment and response; reluctance of individuals to bring children to be vaccinated due to fear of infection; barriers to travel due to local physical distancing measures; disruptions in vaccine supply chains; lack of personal protective equipment; and decisions to stop or postpone vaccination campaigns to reduce the risk of transmission during such campaigns.
evidence: Statement of reasons for disruption based on observed circumstances during the pandemic.

claim: The World Health Organization issued guidance in March 2020 recommending temporary suspension of mass vaccination campaigns but continuation of routine immunisation services.
source: The World Health Organization (WHO) issued guidance in March 2020 on immunisation activities during the COVID-19 pandemic (WHO, 2020b). The guidance recommended a temporary suspension of mass vaccination campaigns, but continuation of routine immunisation services by the health systems while maintaining physical distancing and infection prevention and control measures for COVID-19.
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO guidance document from 2020.

claim: Routine immunisation was one of the most disrupted services relative to other essential health services based on a WHO pulse survey in May and June 2020.
source: Routine immunisation was one of the most disrupted services relative to other essential health services based on a WHO pulse survey in May and June 2020 that was focused on continuity of essential health services during the COVID-19 pandemic (WHO, 2020c).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO pulse survey data.

claim: WHO, UNICEF, Gavi, and partners conducted two pulse polls in April and June 2020 to understand COVID-19-related disruptions to immunisation services.
source: WHO, UNICEF, Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, and their partners also conducted two pulse polls in April and June 2020 to understand COVID-19-related disruptions to immunisation services (WHO, 2020d).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO document describing the pulse polls.

claim: Pulse polls from 82 countries indicated widespread disruption to routine immunisation services in addition to suspension of mass vaccination campaigns.
source: Based on respondents from 82 countries, pulse polls indicated that there was widespread disruption to routine immunisation services in addition to the suspension of mass vaccination campaigns.
evidence: Based on data from pulse polls cited in the previous sentence.

claim: The main reasons for immunisation disruption were low availability of personal protective equipment for healthcare workers, low availability of health workers, and travel restrictions.
source: The main reasons reported for this disruption were low availability of personal protective equipment for healthcare workers, low availability of health workers, and travel restrictions.
evidence: Based on findings from the pulse polls mentioned in the preceding text.

claim: Disruptions to routine health care due to the COVID-19 pandemic are projected to increase child and maternal deaths in low-income and middle-income countries.
source: Disruptions to routine health care due to the COVID-19 pandemic are projected to increase child and maternal deaths in low-income and middle-income countries (Roberton et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Roberton et al. 2020 study.

claim: No country has made a policy decision to stop routine immunisation during a COVID-19 epidemic.
source: No country has made a policy decision to stop routine immunisation during a COVID-19 epidemic.
evidence: Statement of observed policy decisions across countries.

claim: Risk-benefit analysis of countries in Africa shows routine immunisation to have far greater benefits than risks even in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: Risk-benefit analysis of countries in Africa shows routine immunisation to have far greater benefits than risks even in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic (LSHTM CMMID COVID-19 Working Group et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to LSHTM CMMID COVID-19 Working Group analysis.

claim: Routine immunisation coverage has dropped in most countries during the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: Nevertheless, routine immunisation coverage has dropped in most countries (WHO, 2020d).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO data on immunisation coverage.

claim: Both fixed post and door-to-door campaigns targeting under 5-year-old children may cause temporary minor increases in total SARS-CoV-2 infections.
source: Modelling indicates that both fixed post and door-to-door campaigns targeting under 5-year-old children may cause temporary minor increases in total SARS-CoV-2 infections (Hagedorn et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hagedorn et al. 2020 modeling study.

claim: Avoiding campaigns during the local peak of SARS-CoV-2 transmission is key to reducing the effect size of SARS-CoV-2 infections from vaccination campaigns.
source: However, avoiding campaigns during the local peak of SARS-CoV-2 transmission is key to reducing the effect size, and SARS-CoV-2 transmission during campaigns can be minimised with good personal protective equipment and limiting movement of vaccinators (Hagedorn et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hagedorn et al. 2020 modeling study.

claim: WHO recommends that countries consider the risk of outbreaks using epidemiological criteria when deciding whether to conduct preventive vaccination campaigns during the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: The WHO recommends that countries consider the risk of outbreaks using epidemiological criteria when deciding whether to conduct preventive vaccination campaigns during the COVID-19 pandemic, but the guidance was not based on any quantitative assessment of transmission risk for either COVID-19 or existing vaccine-preventable diseases (WHO, 2020e).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO guidance document.

claim: WHO guidance on vaccination campaigns during COVID-19 was not based on any quantitative assessment of transmission risk for either COVID-19 or existing vaccine-preventable diseases.
source: The WHO recommends that countries consider the risk of outbreaks using epidemiological criteria when deciding whether to conduct preventive vaccination campaigns during the COVID-19 pandemic, but the guidance was not based on any quantitative assessment of transmission risk for either COVID-19 or existing vaccine-preventable diseases (WHO, 2020e).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO guidance document and statement about its basis.

claim: Countries need to assess the health impact of postponing vaccination campaigns to inform epidemiological risk assessment for outbreaks due to campaign delays.
source: Hence, countries need to assess the health impact of postponing vaccination campaigns, which can inform the epidemiological risk assessment for outbreaks due to campaign delays and prioritise which vaccines to use in campaigns (WHO, 2020f).
evidence: Logical inference from the need for evidence-based decision making, supported by WHO citation.

claim: The need for health impact assessments of postponing vaccination campaigns is greatest in low- and lower middle-income countries.
source: The need for such assessments is greatest in low- and lower middle-income countries which generally have greater risks of vaccine-preventable disease outbreaks and limited health care resources to deal with COVID-19 epidemics.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about disease burden and healthcare resources in different income settings.

claim: Low- and lower middle-income countries generally have greater risks of vaccine-preventable disease outbreaks and limited health care resources to deal with COVID-19 epidemics.
source: The need for such assessments is greatest in low- and lower middle-income countries which generally have greater risks of vaccine-preventable disease outbreaks and limited health care resources to deal with COVID-19 epidemics.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about disease epidemiology and healthcare infrastructure in different income settings.

claim: Transmission dynamic models were used to project alternative scenarios about postponing vaccination campaigns alongside disruption of routine immunisation for measles, meningococcal A, and yellow fever.
source: To address this, we used transmission dynamic models to project alternative scenarios about postponing vaccination campaigns alongside disruption of routine immunisation, for three pathogens with high outbreak potential and for which mass vaccination campaigns are a key delivery mode alongside routine immunisation – measles, meningococcal A, and yellow fever.
evidence: Description of the study methodology.

claim: Measles, meningococcal A, and yellow fever are pathogens with high outbreak potential for which mass vaccination campaigns are a key delivery mode alongside routine immunisation.
source: To address this, we used transmission dynamic models to project alternative scenarios about postponing vaccination campaigns alongside disruption of routine immunisation, for three pathogens with high outbreak potential and for which mass vaccination campaigns are a key delivery mode alongside routine immunisation – measles, meningococcal A, and yellow fever.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about these pathogens and vaccination strategies.

claim: Deaths and DALYs due to measles, meningococcal A, and yellow fever were projected in 10 low- and lower middle-income countries over 2020-2030.
source: Deaths and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) due to measles, meningococcal A, and yellow fever under different routine and campaign vaccination scenarios were projected in a subset of 10 low- and lower middle-income countries over the years 2020–2030.
evidence: Description of the study methodology and scope.

claim: Three models were used for measles projections.
source: Projections were made using previously validated transmission dynamic models; we used three models for measles, two models for meningococcal A, and two models for yellow fever (summary model details are available in Table 1a-c with full model details in Appendix Section 3; a description of the key drivers of similarities and differences between models is given in Appendix Section 4).
evidence: Description of the study methodology.

claim: Two models were used for meningococcal A projections.
source: Projections were made using previously validated transmission dynamic models; we used three models for measles, two models for meningococcal A, and two models for yellow fever (summary model details are available in Table 1a-c with full model details in Appendix Section 3; a description of the key drivers of similarities and differences between models is given in Appendix Section 4).
evidence: Description of the study methodology.

claim: Two models were used for yellow fever projections.
source: Projections were made using previously validated transmission dynamic models; we used three models for measles, two models for meningococcal A, and two models for yellow fever (summary model details are available in Table 1a-c with full model details in Appendix Section 3; a description of the key drivers of similarities and differences between models is given in Appendix Section 4).
evidence: Description of the study methodology.

claim: Models used routine and campaign vaccination coverage from WUENIC and post campaign surveys for 2000-2019.
source: Models used routine and campaign vaccination coverage from WUENIC (WHO and UNICEF Estimates of National Immunization Coverage) and post campaign surveys for 2000–2019 (Li et al., 2021), and future projections of routine coverage based on assumptions agreed with disease and immunisation programme experts at the global, regional, and national levels (see Appendix 1—table 16).
evidence: Description of data sources used in the models, supported by citation.

claim: Future projections of routine coverage were based on assumptions agreed with disease and immunisation programme experts at global, regional, and national levels.
source: Models used routine and campaign vaccination coverage from WUENIC (WHO and UNICEF Estimates of National Immunization Coverage) and post campaign surveys for 2000–2019 (Li et al., 2021), and future projections of routine coverage based on assumptions agreed with disease and immunisation programme experts at the global, regional, and national levels (see Appendix 1—table 16).
evidence: Description of methodology for determining future coverage assumptions.

claim: Four scenarios were explored that assumed different levels of disruption in 2020 to routine immunisation and postponement of campaigns due to COVID-19.
source: We explored four scenarios that assumed different levels of disruption in the year 2020 to routine immunisation and postponement of campaigns projected in the scenarios, due to COVID-19 (see Table 2).
evidence: Description of the study design and scenarios modeled.

claim: The disruption scenarios are based on 50% reduction in routine immunisation and/or suspension of campaign vaccination in 2020 and postponement to 2021.
source: The disruption scenarios are based on 50% reduction in routine immunisation and/or suspension of campaign vaccination in 2020 and postponement to 2021.
evidence: Description of the specific disruption scenarios modeled.

claim: Disruption scenarios aimed to approximate plausible drops in routine coverage levels and plausible delays to campaigns due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: These disruption scenarios aimed to approximate plausible drops in routine coverage levels and plausible delays to campaigns due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
evidence: Explanation of the rationale for the chosen disruption scenarios.

claim: The counterfactual comparative scenario (BAU) is sustaining immunisation services at coverage projections made prior to COVID-19 without any disruption.
source: Our counterfactual comparative scenario was sustaining immunisation services at coverage projections made prior to COVID-19 (i.e. without any disruption).
evidence: Description of the baseline scenario for comparison.

claim: Reduced routine vaccination coverage in 2020 without catch-up vaccination may lead to an increase in measles and yellow fever disease burden in the modelled countries.
source: Reduced routine vaccination coverage in 2020 without catch-up vaccination may lead to an increase in measles and yellow fever disease burden in the modelled countries.
evidence: Summary of modeling results presented in the abstract.

claim: Delaying planned campaigns in Ethiopia and Nigeria by a year may significantly increase the risk of measles outbreaks.
source: Delaying planned campaigns in Ethiopia and Nigeria by a year may significantly increase the risk of measles outbreaks (both countries did complete their supplementary immunisation activities (SIAs) planned for 2020).
evidence: Summary of modeling results presented in the abstract.

claim: Both Ethiopia and Nigeria completed their supplementary immunisation activities planned for 2020.
source: Delaying planned campaigns in Ethiopia and Nigeria by a year may significantly increase the risk of measles outbreaks (both countries did complete their supplementary immunisation activities (SIAs) planned for 2020).
evidence: Factual statement about what actually occurred in these countries.

claim: For yellow fever vaccination, delay in campaigns leads to a potential disease burden rise of >1 death per 100,000 people per year until the campaigns are implemented.
source: For yellow fever vaccination, delay in campaigns leads to a potential disease burden rise of >1 death per 100,000 people per year until the campaigns are implemented.
evidence: Summary of modeling results presented in the abstract.

claim: For meningococcal A vaccination, short-term disruptions in 2020 are unlikely to have a significant impact due to the persistence of direct and indirect benefits from past introductory campaigns of the 1- to 29-year-old population.
source: For meningococcal A vaccination, short-term disruptions in 2020 are unlikely to have a significant impact due to the persistence of direct and indirect benefits from past introductory campaigns of the 1- to 29-year-old population, bolstered by inclusion of the vaccine into the routine immunisation schedule accompanied by further catch-up campaigns.
evidence: Summary of modeling results and interpretation presented in the abstract.

claim: The impact of COVID-19-related disruption to vaccination programs varies between infections and countries.
source: The impact of COVID-19-related disruption to vaccination programs varies between infections and countries.
evidence: Summary conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: Planning and implementation of campaigns should consider country and infection-specific epidemiological factors and local immunity gaps worsened by the COVID-19 pandemic when prioritising vaccines and strategies for catch-up vaccination.
source: Planning and implementation of campaigns should consider country and infection-specific epidemiological factors and local immunity gaps worsened by the COVID-19 pandemic when prioritising vaccines and strategies for catch-up vaccination.
evidence: Recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: The health impact varies across the disruption scenarios for the three infections in the different countries.
source: The health impact varies across the disruption scenarios for the three infections in the different countries.
evidence: Summary statement of results section findings.

claim: Bangladesh initially postponed its measles campaign by a few months.
source: In the case of measles, Bangladesh initially postponed its campaign by a few months.
evidence: Factual statement about what occurred in Bangladesh.

claim: The Penn State model predicts that delaying the 2020 measles campaign in Bangladesh increases deaths slightly (by 0.03 per 100,000 over 2020-2030).
source: The Penn State model predicts that delaying the 2020 campaign increases deaths slightly (by 0.03 per 100,000 over 2020–2030) but this increase is not seen in DynaMICE.
evidence: Specific modeling result from the Penn State model.

claim: DynaMICE does not predict an increase in deaths from delaying the 2020 measles campaign in Bangladesh.
source: The Penn State model predicts that delaying the 2020 campaign increases deaths slightly (by 0.03 per 100,000 over 2020–2030) but this increase is not seen in DynaMICE.
evidence: Specific modeling result from the DynaMICE model.

claim: DynaMICE predicts an increase in deaths of 0.35 per 100,000 over 2020-2030 in Bangladesh if routine coverage drops by 50%.
source: Conversely, DynaMICE predicts an increase in deaths of 0.35 per 100,000 over 2020–2030 if routine coverage drops by 50%, but this is not seen in the Penn State model; see Appendix 1—table 2 for further details.
evidence: Specific modeling result from the DynaMICE model.

claim: The Penn State model does not predict an increase in deaths in Bangladesh if routine coverage drops by 50%.
source: Conversely, DynaMICE predicts an increase in deaths of 0.35 per 100,000 over 2020–2030 if routine coverage drops by 50%, but this is not seen in the Penn State model; see Appendix 1—table 2 for further details.
evidence: Specific modeling result from the Penn State model.

claim: For Ethiopia, a reduction in routine coverage is predicted to lead to outbreaks sooner and increases in overall deaths in all three models (DynaMICE, Penn State models and IDM).
source: For Ethiopia, a reduction in routine coverage is predicted to lead to outbreaks sooner and increases in overall deaths in all three models (DynaMICE, Penn State models and IDM), while postponing the 2020 campaign only increases deaths in the DynaMICE model.
evidence: Summary of modeling results from three different models for Ethiopia.

claim: For Ethiopia, postponing the 2020 measles campaign only increases deaths in the DynaMICE model.
source: For Ethiopia, a reduction in routine coverage is predicted to lead to outbreaks sooner and increases in overall deaths in all three models (DynaMICE, Penn State models and IDM), while postponing the 2020 campaign only increases deaths in the DynaMICE model.
evidence: Specific modeling result comparing different models for Ethiopia.

claim: The Ethiopian measles campaign was eventually reinstated only 3 months later than scheduled.
source: The Ethiopian campaign was eventually reinstated only 3 months later than scheduled.
evidence: Factual statement about what occurred in Ethiopia.

claim: For Kenya, the disruption to routine and campaign immunisation was not predicted to lead to increased risk of measles outbreaks due to high coverage of the first dose of measles vaccine and better optimally-timed campaigns.
source: For Kenya, the disruption to routine and campaign immunisation was not predicted to lead to increased risk of outbreaks, due to high coverage of the first dose of measles vaccine and better optimally-timed campaigns in preventing outbreaks during 2020–2030, although coverage of the second-dose of measles vaccine is suboptimal.
evidence: Summary of modeling results for Kenya with explanation of the underlying reasons.

claim: In Kenya, coverage of the second-dose of measles vaccine is suboptimal.
source: For Kenya, the disruption to routine and campaign immunisation was not predicted to lead to increased risk of outbreaks, due to high coverage of the first dose of measles vaccine and better optimally-timed campaigns in preventing outbreaks during 2020–2030, although coverage of the second-dose of measles vaccine is suboptimal.
evidence: Statement about vaccination coverage in Kenya.

claim: For Nigeria, either postponement of the 2020 immunisation campaign or a reduction in routine coverage is predicted to lead to increases in measles mortality in Penn State and IDM models, but not in DynaMICE.
source: For Nigeria, either postponement of the 2020 immunisation campaign or a reduction in routine coverage is predicted to lead to increases in measles mortality in Penn State and IDM models, but not in DynaMICE.
evidence: Summary of modeling results from three different models for Nigeria.

claim: The increases in measles mortality predicted for Nigeria were highly localised in the subnational IDM model.
source: Note that these increases were predicted to be highly localised in the subnational IDM model; see Discussion for details.
evidence: Specific detail about the IDM model results for Nigeria.

claim: For South Sudan, the postponement of immunisation campaigns from 2020 to 2021 is predicted to be beneficial in averting a potential outbreak in 2022 in both DynaMICE and Penn State models.
source: For South Sudan, the postponement of immunisation campaigns from 2020 to 2021 is predicted to be beneficial in averting a potential outbreak in 2022 in both DynaMICE and Penn State models (although note caveats in the Discussion about such predictions), but decreases in routine coverage are predicted to lead to more deaths, with a larger predicted increase in DynaMICE.
evidence: Summary of modeling results from two models for South Sudan.

claim: For South Sudan, decreases in routine coverage are predicted to lead to more measles deaths, with a larger predicted increase in DynaMICE.
source: For South Sudan, the postponement of immunisation campaigns from 2020 to 2021 is predicted to be beneficial in averting a potential outbreak in 2022 in both DynaMICE and Penn State models (although note caveats in the Discussion about such predictions), but decreases in routine coverage are predicted to lead to more deaths, with a larger predicted increase in DynaMICE.
evidence: Summary of modeling results comparing two models for South Sudan.

claim: For Chad, both DynaMICE and Penn State models predict an overall increase in measles deaths with routine coverage drops.
source: For Chad, both DynaMICE and Penn State models predict an overall increase in deaths with routine coverage drops, but only the Penn State model predicts an increase with a postponement of campaigns.
evidence: Summary of modeling results from two models for Chad.

claim: For Chad, only the Penn State model predicts an increase in measles deaths with a postponement of campaigns.
source: For Chad, both DynaMICE and Penn State models predict an overall increase in deaths with routine coverage drops, but only the Penn State model predicts an increase with a postponement of campaigns.
evidence: Specific comparison of modeling results between two models for Chad.

claim: Short-term disruption to routine immunisation in Burkina Faso, Niger, Nigeria, and Chad would not have a significant impact on meningococcal A disease incidence.
source: In the case of meningococcal A (MenA), the short-term disruption to routine immunisation in Burkina Faso, Niger, Nigeria, and Chad, as well as the short-term disruption of immunisation campaigns in Nigeria and Chad would not have a significant impact on the disease incidence (see Appendix 1—table 4 for model-specific estimates by country).
evidence: Summary of modeling results for meningococcal A across multiple countries.

claim: Short-term disruption of meningococcal A immunisation campaigns in Nigeria and Chad would not have a significant impact on disease incidence.
source: In the case of meningococcal A (MenA), the short-term disruption to routine immunisation in Burkina Faso, Niger, Nigeria, and Chad, as well as the short-term disruption of immunisation campaigns in Nigeria and Chad would not have a significant impact on the disease incidence (see Appendix 1—table 4 for model-specific estimates by country).
evidence: Summary of modeling results for meningococcal A in specific countries.

claim: Burkina Faso, Niger, Nigeria, and Chad conducted mass preventive meningococcal A campaigns targeting 1- to 29-year-old populations between 2010 and 2014.
source: These four countries conducted mass preventive campaigns targeting 1- to 29-year-old populations between 2010 and 2014, and introduced the vaccine into their routine immunization schedules between 2016 and 2019.
evidence: Factual statement about vaccination campaigns in these countries.

claim: Burkina Faso, Niger, Nigeria, and Chad introduced meningococcal A vaccine into their routine immunization schedules between 2016 and 2019.
source: These four countries conducted mass preventive campaigns targeting 1- to 29-year-old populations between 2010 and 2014, and introduced the vaccine into their routine immunization schedules between 2016 and 2019.
evidence: Factual statement about vaccination program implementation in these countries.

claim: Niger and Burkina Faso completed catch-up campaigns concomitantly with the introduction of meningococcal A vaccine into routine.
source: Niger and Burkina Faso completed catch-up campaigns concomitantly with the introduction into routine, and Chad and Nigeria have started but not completed their catch-up campaigns.
evidence: Factual statement about vaccination program implementation in these countries.

claim: Chad and Nigeria have started but not completed their meningococcal A catch-up campaigns.
source: Niger and Burkina Faso completed catch-up campaigns concomitantly with the introduction into routine, and Chad and Nigeria have started but not completed their catch-up campaigns.
evidence: Factual statement about vaccination program status in these countries.

claim: A maximum of a 4% increase in meningococcal A deaths over the long term is projected in either of the models with minimal change in the short term of within 5 years.
source: A maximum of a 4% increase in MenA deaths over the long term is projected in either of the models and with minimal change in the short term of within 5 years.
evidence: Summary of modeling results for meningococcal A.

claim: The minimal impact of meningococcal A disruptions is because of the persistence of protection against MenA due to the vaccination strategy combining mass vaccination campaign and routine introduction, which led to a lasting interruption of transmission.
source: This is because of the persistence of protection against MenA due to the vaccination strategy combining mass vaccination campaign and routine introduction, which led to a lasting interruption of transmission, in particular from the direct and indirect effects of the initial mass campaigns of the 1- to 29-year-old population in 2010–2014.
evidence: Explanation of the mechanism behind the modeling results, based on understanding of vaccine-induced immunity and transmission dynamics.

claim: For the Democratic Republic of Congo and Nigeria, the postponement of yellow fever immunisation campaigns from 2020 to 2021 was predicted to cause a short-term increase in burden.
source: In the case of yellow fever, for the Democratic Republic of Congo and Nigeria, the postponement of immunisation campaigns from 2020 to 2021 was predicted to cause a short-term increase in burden but when campaigns were implemented, the overall burden was reduced for the time period.
evidence: Summary of modeling results for yellow fever in specific countries.

claim: For the Democratic Republic of Congo and Nigeria, when yellow fever campaigns were implemented after postponement, the overall burden was reduced for the time period 2020-2030.
source: In the case of yellow fever, for the Democratic Republic of Congo and Nigeria, the postponement of immunisation campaigns from 2020 to 2021 was predicted to cause a short-term increase in burden but when campaigns were implemented, the overall burden was reduced for the time period.
evidence: Summary of modeling results for yellow fever in specific countries.

claim: For the Democratic Republic of Congo and Nigeria, a reduction in routine yellow fever immunization during 2020 was predicted to increase burden over the period 2020-2030.
source: A reduction in routine immunization during 2020 was predicted to increase burden over the same period 2020–2030.
evidence: Summary of modeling results for yellow fever in specific countries.

claim: For Ghana, the postponement of yellow fever immunisation campaigns from 2020 to 2021 did not lead to an increase in yellow fever burden in the short-term.
source: For Ghana, the postponement of immunisation campaigns from 2020 to 2021 did not lead to an increase in yellow fever burden in the short-term, whereas a reduction in routine immunization in 2020 was predicted to increase the yellow fever burden by 0.33 or 0.07 deaths per 100,000 between 2020 and 2030 in the Imperial and Notre Dame models respectively.
evidence: Summary of modeling results for yellow fever in Ghana.

claim: For Ghana, a reduction in routine yellow fever immunization in 2020 was predicted to increase the yellow fever burden by 0.33 deaths per 100,000 between 2020 and 2030 in the Imperial model.
source: For Ghana, the postponement of immunisation campaigns from 2020 to 2021 did not lead to an increase in yellow fever burden in the short-term, whereas a reduction in routine immunization in 2020 was predicted to increase the yellow fever burden by 0.33 or 0.07 deaths per 100,000 between 2020 and 2030 in the Imperial and Notre Dame models respectively.
evidence: Specific modeling result from the Imperial model for Ghana.

claim: For Ghana, a reduction in routine yellow fever immunization in 2020 was predicted to increase the yellow fever burden by 0.07 deaths per 100,000 between 2020 and 2030 in the Notre Dame model.
source: For Ghana, the postponement of immunisation campaigns from 2020 to 2021 did not lead to an increase in yellow fever burden in the short-term, whereas a reduction in routine immunization in 2020 was predicted to increase the yellow fever burden by 0.33 or 0.07 deaths per 100,000 between 2020 and 2030 in the Imperial and Notre Dame models respectively.
evidence: Specific modeling result from the Notre Dame model for Ghana.

claim: Neither yellow fever model was designed to specifically capture yellow fever outbreak dynamics.
source: Neither model was designed to specifically capture yellow fever outbreak dynamics.
evidence: Statement about the limitations of the models used.

claim: The delay of yellow fever immunisation campaigns was predicted to reduce the burden of yellow fever for 2020-2030 in select settings by a small (less than 1%) amount.
source: Therefore, although the delay of immunisation campaigns was predicted to reduce the burden of yellow fever for 2020–2030 in select settings by a small (less than 1%) amount, the increased risk of an outbreak is not accounted for in the models and this could outweigh the predicted long-term benefits.
evidence: Summary of modeling results with caveat about model limitations.

claim: The increased risk of a yellow fever outbreak from campaign delays is not accounted for in the models and this could outweigh the predicted long-term benefits of delayed campaigns.
source: Therefore, although the delay of immunisation campaigns was predicted to reduce the burden of yellow fever for 2020–2030 in select settings by a small (less than 1%) amount, the increased risk of an outbreak is not accounted for in the models and this could outweigh the predicted long-term benefits.
evidence: Statement about model limitations and their implications for interpreting results.

claim: The scale of excess mortality due to immunisation service disruptions are higher for measles vaccination in comparison to meningococcal A and yellow fever vaccination.
source: The scale of excess mortality due to the immunisation service disruptions are higher for measles vaccination in comparison to meningococcal A and yellow fever vaccination; indeed excess mortality is minimal for meningococcal A.
evidence: Summary statement based on Figure 2 showing excess deaths across pathogens.

claim: Excess mortality from meningococcal A vaccination disruptions is minimal.
source: The scale of excess mortality due to the immunisation service disruptions are higher for measles vaccination in comparison to meningococcal A and yellow fever vaccination; indeed excess mortality is minimal for meningococcal A.
evidence: Summary statement based on Figure 2 showing excess deaths across pathogens.

claim: For measles, a 50% reduction in routine immunisation was projected to increase the excess deaths the most in comparison to scenarios involving the postponement of immunisation campaigns from 2020 to 2021.
source: For measles, there are differences between models but usually a 50% reduction in routine immunisation was projected to increase the excess deaths the most in comparison to scenarios involving the postponement of immunisation campaigns from 2020 to 2021.
evidence: Summary of modeling results across different scenarios for measles.

claim: For MenA, a 50% reduction in routine immunisation and the postponement of immunisation campaigns from 2020 to 2021 was projected to increase the excess deaths the most for Chad.
source: For MenA, a 50% reduction in routine immunisation and the postponement of immunisation campaigns from 2020 to 2021 was projected to increase the excess deaths the most for Chad, although the scale of absolute impact is minimal (see Figure 2).
evidence: Summary of modeling results for MenA in Chad, referencing Figure 2.

claim: For yellow fever, a reduction in routine immunisation was projected to increase the excess deaths the most (either in conjunction with campaign delay or not).
source: For yellow fever, a reduction in routine immunisation was projected to increase the excess deaths the most (either in conjunction with campaign delay or not).
evidence: Summary of modeling results across different scenarios for yellow fever.

claim: The beneficial effect of postponing yellow fever campaigns in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is due solely to the proportionally larger campaign implemented in 2021, as a campaign with the same coverage leads to more fully vaccinated persons as the population grows.
source: The beneficial effect is due solely to the proportionally larger campaign implemented in 2021, that is a campaign with the same coverage leads to more fully vaccinated persons as the population grows.
evidence: Explanation of the mechanism behind the modeling result.

claim: The health impact of routine immunisation service disruptions and mass vaccination campaign suspensions due to the COVID-19 pandemic differs widely between infections and countries.
source: The health impact of routine immunisation service disruptions and mass vaccination campaign suspensions due to the COVID-19 pandemic differs widely between infections and countries, so decision-makers need to consider their local epidemiological situation.
evidence: Summary conclusion from the study results.

claim: For meningococcal A and yellow fever, postponing campaigns has a minimal short-term effect because both pathogens have a low effective reproduction number and strong existing herd immunity from recent campaigns in the countries modelled.
source: For meningococcal A and yellow fever, we predict that postponing campaigns has a minimal short-term effect because both pathogens have a low effective reproduction number and strong existing herd immunity from recent campaigns in the countries modelled (see Appendix 1—table 17 for list of campaigns).
evidence: Summary of modeling results with explanation of the underlying epidemiological reasons.

claim: The prediction that postponing meningococcal A and yellow fever campaigns has minimal short-term effect is influenced by the model structures and their propensity to capture outbreak dynamics, which particularly affects the predictions for yellow fever.
source: However, this is influenced by the model structures and their propensity to capture outbreak dynamics, which particularly affects the predictions for yellow fever.
evidence: Statement about model limitations and their influence on results.

claim: For measles, in some countries such as Ethiopia and Nigeria, even a 1-year postponement of immunisation campaigns could have led to large outbreaks.
source: For measles, in some countries such as Ethiopia and Nigeria, even a 1-year postponement of immunisation campaigns could have led to large outbreaks, but both countries were able to implement planned SIAs in 2020 after a few months' delay.
evidence: Summary of modeling results for specific countries.

claim: Ethiopia and Nigeria were able to implement planned measles SIAs in 2020 after a few months' delay.
source: For measles, in some countries such as Ethiopia and Nigeria, even a 1-year postponement of immunisation campaigns could have led to large outbreaks, but both countries were able to implement planned SIAs in 2020 after a few months' delay.
evidence: Factual statement about what occurred in these countries.

claim: In countries with high routine immunisation coverage and/or recent campaigns, measles SIAs may be postponed by a year without causing large outbreaks.
source: In other countries with high routine immunisation coverage and/or recent campaigns, SIAs may be postponed by a year without causing large outbreaks.
evidence: Summary of modeling results for countries with different epidemiological contexts.

claim: Model projections about future measles outbreaks differ between models in terms of both timing and magnitude.
source: However, model projections about future outbreaks differ between models in terms of both timing and magnitude.
evidence: Statement about variability in model predictions.

claim: Differences in model projections capture uncertainty around data and model structure that differ between models.
source: These differences capture uncertainty around data and model structure that differ between models.
evidence: Explanation of the source of variability in model predictions.

claim: In some modelled scenarios, postponement of immunisation campaigns does not appear to increase overall cases if the delay time-period is less than the interval to the next outbreak.
source: In some of our modelled scenarios, postponement of immunisation campaigns does not appear to increase overall cases, if the delay time-period is less than the interval to the next outbreak.
evidence: Summary of specific modeling results under certain conditions.

claim: The finding that postponement of campaigns may not increase cases does not imply that a postponement is preferred, as other contextual or programmatic factors are not taken into account.
source: This does not imply that a postponement is preferred, as we do not take into account other contextual or programmatic factors; rather it reflects the effectiveness of campaigns in closing the immunity gaps and the demographic effect of including more children in delayed campaigns.
evidence: Clarification about the interpretation of modeling results and their limitations.

claim: The finding that postponement may not increase cases reflects the effectiveness of campaigns in closing immunity gaps and the demographic effect of including more children in delayed campaigns.
source: This does not imply that a postponement is preferred, as we do not take into account other contextual or programmatic factors; rather it reflects the effectiveness of campaigns in closing the immunity gaps and the demographic effect of including more children in delayed campaigns.
evidence: Explanation of the mechanisms behind the modeling results.

claim: In instances with very low routine immunisation coverage, the vaccination campaign is the main opportunity for missed children to be vaccinated.
source: In instances with very low routine immunisation coverage, there is a possibility that the vaccination campaign is the main opportunity for missed children to be vaccinated.
evidence: Logical inference about the role of campaigns in low-coverage settings.

claim: For the same proportion of the same age group targeted by campaigns, more children will be vaccinated for the same coverage levels in countries with birth rates increasing over time.
source: Thus, for the same proportion of the same age group targeted by campaigns, more children will be vaccinated for the same coverage levels in countries with birth rates increasing over time.
evidence: Logical inference about the demographic effects on vaccination numbers.

claim: There is considerable uncertainty around both model findings and data inputs such as incidence and vaccine coverage.
source: While these results may be useful in the COVID-19 context, there is also considerable uncertainty around both model findings and data inputs such as incidence and vaccine coverage that prohibits further general comment on the optimal timing of campaigns.
evidence: Statement about limitations of the study.

claim: The measles immunisation campaigns for 2020 in Nigeria were specifically targeted at Kogi and Niger states.
source: The measles immunisation campaigns for 2020 in Nigeria were specifically targeted at Kogi and Niger states, states that were originally scheduled for inclusion in the campaigns for 2019 across northern Nigeria which were delayed for other reasons.
evidence: Factual statement about the specific vaccination campaigns in Nigeria.

claim: Kogi and Niger states in Nigeria were originally scheduled for inclusion in measles campaigns for 2019 across northern Nigeria which were delayed for other reasons.
source: The measles immunisation campaigns for 2020 in Nigeria were specifically targeted at Kogi and Niger states, states that were originally scheduled for inclusion in the campaigns for 2019 across northern Nigeria which were delayed for other reasons.
evidence: Factual statement about the history of vaccination campaigns in Nigeria.

claim: IDM's subnational Nigeria model indicated that further campaign delays would result in a high risk of localised outbreaks in Kogi and Niger states due to localised build-up of susceptibility from low routine immunisation coverage and long window between campaigns.
source: Given the localised build-up of susceptibility in these two states due to low routine immunisation coverage and the long window between campaigns, IDM's subnational Nigeria model indicated that further campaign delays would result in a high risk of localised outbreaks in these states (one potential explanation for the IDM model predicting worse consequences of delays in these campaigns than the other models).
evidence: Specific modeling result from the IDM model for Nigeria with explanation.

claim: Campaigns targeted specifically to Kogi and Niger states in Nigeria were implemented in October 2020.
source: Campaigns targeted specifically to these two states were implemented in October 2020.
evidence: Factual statement about what occurred in Nigeria.

claim: For countries where routine immunisation coverage was low even before the COVID-19 pandemic, the build-up of the susceptible population from low routine immunisation coverage over 2-3 years between campaigns enhances the risk of outbreaks more than recent and temporary disruptions to routine immunisation.
source: In general, for countries where routine immunisation coverage was low even before the COVID-19 pandemic, the build-up of the susceptible population from low routine immunisation coverage over 2–3 years between campaigns enhances the risk of outbreaks more than recent and temporary disruptions to routine immunisation.
evidence: General conclusion based on modeling results and epidemiological understanding.

claim: The models did not include the possibility that COVID-19 restrictions may have temporarily reduced measles transmissibility and the risk of measles outbreaks due to reduced chance of introduction of infection into populations with immunity gaps.
source: Further, our models did not include the possibility that COVID-19 restrictions may have temporarily reduced measles transmissibility and the risk of measles outbreaks due to reduced chance of introduction of infection into populations with immunity gaps.
evidence: Statement about a limitation of the models.

claim: The risk of measles outbreaks rises again rapidly once travel restrictions and physical distancing are relaxed.
source: This risk rises again rapidly once travel restrictions and physical distancing are relaxed.
evidence: Inference about disease dynamics when restrictions are lifted.

claim: The rapid rise in measles outbreak risk once COVID-19 restrictions are lifted is an additional reason for implementing postponed immunisation campaigns at the earliest opportunity.
source: This is an additional reason (which we do not model) for implementing postponed immunisation campaigns at the earliest opportunity to prevent measles outbreaks as COVID-19 restrictions are lifted (LSHTM CMMID COVID-19 Working Group et al., 2021).
evidence: Recommendation based on inference about disease dynamics, supported by citation.

claim: The models generally show that reductions in routine immunisation coverage have a far greater impact on predicted excess deaths over the next decade for all infections modeled than postponement of campaigns.
source: While the degree of health impact of service disruptions varies, the models generally show that reductions in routine immunisation coverage have a far greater impact on predicted excess deaths over the next decade for all infections modeled than postponement of campaigns.
evidence: Summary conclusion from modeling results across all pathogens.

claim: The finding that reductions in routine immunisation have greater impact than campaign postponement has significant implications for countries planning catch-up strategies.
source: This has significant implications for countries planning catch-up strategies and highlights the need for increased emphasis on the importance of implementing catch-up as an ongoing part of routine immunisation (WHO, 2020f).
evidence: Inference about policy implications based on modeling results, supported by WHO citation.

claim: The disease burden averted by measles and meningococcal A vaccination are primarily among under-5-year-old and under-10-year-old children respectively.
source: The disease burden averted by measles and meningococcal A vaccination are primarily among under-5-year-old and under-10-year-old children respectively, and disease burden averted by yellow fever vaccination are among younger age-group individuals.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge about disease epidemiology.

claim: Disease burden averted by yellow fever vaccination are among younger age-group individuals.
source: The disease burden averted by measles and meningococcal A vaccination are primarily among under-5-year-old and under-10-year-old children respectively, and disease burden averted by yellow fever vaccination are among younger age-group individuals.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge about disease epidemiology.

claim: Children and younger age-group individuals are at relatively lower risk of morbidity and mortality from COVID-19 in comparison to elderly populations.
source: Since children and younger age-group individuals are at relatively lower risk of morbidity and mortality from COVID-19 in comparison to elderly populations, the health benefits of sustaining measles, meningococcal A, and yellow fever immunisation programmes during the COVID-19 pandemic outweigh the excess SARS-CoV-2 infection risk to these age groups that are associated with vaccination service delivery points.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge about COVID-19 epidemiology.

claim: The health benefits of sustaining measles, meningococcal A, and yellow fever immunisation programmes during the COVID-19 pandemic outweigh the excess SARS-CoV-2 infection risk to children and younger age groups associated with vaccination service delivery points.
source: Since children and younger age-group individuals are at relatively lower risk of morbidity and mortality from COVID-19 in comparison to elderly populations, the health benefits of sustaining measles, meningococcal A, and yellow fever immunisation programmes during the COVID-19 pandemic outweigh the excess SARS-CoV-2 infection risk to these age groups that are associated with vaccination service delivery points.
evidence: Conclusion based on inference from modeling results and knowledge about COVID-19 risk by age.

claim: The delivery of measles, meningococcal A, and yellow fever immunisation services should continue during the COVID-19 pandemic by adapting service delivery in a COVID-secure manner with implementation of SARS-CoV-2 infection prevention and control measures.
source: Thereby, the delivery of measles, meningococcal A, and yellow fever immunisation services should continue, as logistically as possible, by adapting service delivery in a COVID-secure manner with implementation of SARS-CoV-2 infection prevention and control measures.
evidence: Recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: The study has not considered logistical constraints posed by the COVID-19 prevention and control measures on vaccine supply, demand for vaccination, access, and health workforce.
source: Our study has limitations and we have not considered logistical constraints posed by the COVID-19 prevention and control measures on vaccine supply, demand for vaccination, access, and health workforce.
evidence: Statement about study limitations.

claim: Future introduction of COVID-19 vaccination may divert the workforce normally conducting campaigns for other vaccines.
source: Future introduction of COVID-19 vaccination may also divert the workforce normally conducting campaigns for other vaccines.
evidence: Speculation about potential future impacts.

claim: The models do not reflect geographical heterogeneity sub-nationally, whereas in reality this is a key feature.
source: Our models do not reflect geographical heterogeneity sub-nationally, whereas in reality this is a key feature.
evidence: Statement about model limitations.

claim: The models do not incorporate known seasonality of infections, which may affect the window of opportunity for catching up.
source: Nor do we incorporate known seasonality of infections, which may affect the window of opportunity for catching up.
evidence: Statement about model limitations.

claim: The models used in this analysis, in particular for yellow fever, are best suited to capture long-term changes in disease burden due to vaccination and cannot capture outbreak dynamics that may arise in the short-term.
source: The models used in this analysis, in particular for yellow fever, are best suited to capture long-term changes in disease burden due to vaccination and cannot capture outbreak dynamics that may arise in the short-term.
evidence: Statement about model limitations and capabilities.

claim: A key strength of the analysis is that two to three models were used for each infection, which allowed investigation of whether projections were sensitive to model structure and assumptions.
source: A key strength of our analysis is that we used two to three models for each infection, which allowed investigation of whether projections were sensitive to model structure and assumptions.
evidence: Statement about study strengths.

claim: Each model had different strengths and limitations.
source: Each model had different strengths and limitations.
evidence: General statement about the models used.

claim: Some models measured epidemic properties like reproduction numbers directly, while other models used estimates from other studies.
source: For instance, some models measured epidemic properties like reproduction numbers directly, while other models used estimates from other studies.
evidence: Description of differences between models.

claim: Quantitative differences were found between models of the same infection.
source: We did indeed find quantitative differences between models of the same infection, but most models agreed on the countries in which disruptions had the largest effect on disease burden.
evidence: Summary of findings from model comparison.

claim: Most models agreed on the countries in which disruptions had the largest effect on disease burden.
source: We did indeed find quantitative differences between models of the same infection, but most models agreed on the countries in which disruptions had the largest effect on disease burden.
evidence: Summary of findings from model comparison.

claim: A limitation is the omission of changes to transmission in the three pathogens due to COVID-19 mitigation measures.
source: A further limitation is the omission of changes to transmission in the three pathogens due to COVID-19 mitigation measures.
evidence: Statement about study limitations.

claim: All three included pathogens have substantially different dynamics to those of SARS-CoV-2.
source: This is a critical area that needs further investigation; however, all three included pathogens have substantially different dynamics to those of SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge about pathogen transmission dynamics.

claim: For yellow fever, the majority of transmission is sylvatic rather than person-to-person.
source: For yellow fever, the majority of transmission is sylvatic rather than person-to-person, so COVID-19 mitigation measures are unlikely to have a major effect on incidence, unless they decrease contact between humans and the sylvatic cycle.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge about yellow fever transmission.

claim: COVID-19 mitigation measures are unlikely to have a major effect on yellow fever incidence, unless they decrease contact between humans and the sylvatic cycle.
source: For yellow fever, the majority of transmission is sylvatic rather than person-to-person, so COVID-19 mitigation measures are unlikely to have a major effect on incidence, unless they decrease contact between humans and the sylvatic cycle.
evidence: Inference based on knowledge about yellow fever transmission and COVID-19 mitigation measures.

claim: For meningococcal A, even with a decrease in vaccine coverage there is limited potential for outbreaks, so decreased transmission due to COVID-19 non-pharmaceutical interventions will only reinforce this.
source: For meningococcal A, we find that even with a decrease in vaccine coverage there is limited potential for outbreaks, so decreased transmission due to COVID-19 non-pharmaceutical interventions will only reinforce this.
evidence: Inference based on modeling results and understanding of how NPIs would affect transmission.

claim: For measles, there is the potential for non-pharmaceutical interventions to decrease transmission.
source: For measles, there is the potential for non-pharmaceutical interventions to decrease transmission.
evidence: Statement based on understanding of measles transmission and NPIs.

claim: Measles is much more transmissible than COVID-19 (with R0 usually well above 10 rather than 2-5).
source: However, measles is much more transmissible than COVID-19 (with R0 usually well above 10 rather than 2–5 Guerra et al., 2017), and transmission is generally concentrated among very young children rather than adults.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge about measles and COVID-19 transmissibility, supported by citation.

claim: Measles transmission is generally concentrated among very young children rather than adults.
source: However, measles is much more transmissible than COVID-19 (with R0 usually well above 10 rather than 2–5 Guerra et al., 2017), and transmission is generally concentrated among very young children rather than adults.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge about measles epidemiology.

claim: It is unclear whether interventions designed for COVID-19 (mask wearing, closure of schools, workplaces and retail, travel restrictions etc.) will be able to prevent measles outbreaks.
source: Hence it is unclear whether interventions designed for COVID-19 (mask wearing, closure of schools, workplaces and retail, travel restrictions etc.) will be able to prevent measles outbreaks.
evidence: Inference based on differences in transmission characteristics between measles and COVID-19.

claim: While COVID-19 mitigation measures may temporarily reduce measles transmissibility and outbreak risk from measles immunity gaps, the risk for measles outbreaks will rise rapidly once COVID-19-related contact restrictions are lifted.
source: Further, while COVID-19 mitigation measures may temporarily reduce measles transmissibility and outbreak risk from measles immunity gaps, the risk for measles outbreaks will rise rapidly once COVID-19-related contact restrictions are lifted (LSHTM CMMID COVID-19 Working Group et al., 2021), which happens at different rates in different parts of countries.
evidence: Inference about disease dynamics when restrictions are lifted, supported by citation.

claim: COVID-19-related contact restrictions are lifted at different rates in different parts of countries.
source: Further, while COVID-19 mitigation measures may temporarily reduce measles transmissibility and outbreak risk from measles immunity gaps, the risk for measles outbreaks will rise rapidly once COVID-19-related contact restrictions are lifted (LSHTM CMMID COVID-19 Working Group et al., 2021), which happens at different rates in different parts of countries.
evidence: Statement based on observed patterns of restriction lifting.

claim: The health impact assessment was conducted to align with the WHO framework for decision making using an evidence-based approach to assist in prioritisation of vaccines and strategies for catch-up vaccination during the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: We conducted our health impact assessment to align with the WHO framework for decision making using an evidence-based approach to assist in prioritisation of vaccines and strategies for catch-up vaccination during the COVID-19 pandemic (WHO, 2020f).
evidence: Statement about the purpose and alignment of the study, supported by WHO citation.

claim: The WHO framework highlights three main steps, with the primary step being an epidemiological risk assessment for each disease based on the burden of disease and population immunity, as well as the risk factors associated with the immunisation service disruptions.
source: The framework highlights three main steps, with the primary step being an epidemiological risk assessment for each disease based on the burden of disease and population immunity, as well as the risk factors associated with the immunisation service disruptions.
evidence: Description of the WHO framework referenced in the previous sentence.

claim: The second step of the WHO framework focuses on the amenability of delivery strategies and operational factors for each vaccine.
source: The second step focuses on the amenability of delivery strategies and operational factors for each vaccine, and the third step on the assessment of contextual factors and competing needs.
evidence: Description of the WHO framework.

claim: The third step of the WHO framework focuses on the assessment of contextual factors and competing needs.
source: The second step focuses on the amenability of delivery strategies and operational factors for each vaccine, and the third step on the assessment of contextual factors and competing needs.
evidence: Description of the WHO framework.

claim: The health impact assessment addresses in part the primary step of an epidemiological risk assessment by estimating the disease burden for different immunisation scenarios.
source: Our health impact assessment addresses in part the primary step of an epidemiological risk assessment by estimating the disease burden for different immunisation scenarios, but does not include the health impact assessment of excess COVID-19 disease burden attributable to these immunisation scenarios.
evidence: Statement about what the study does and does not address.

claim: The health impact assessment does not include the health impact assessment of excess COVID-19 disease burden attributable to the immunisation scenarios.
source: Our health impact assessment addresses in part the primary step of an epidemiological risk assessment by estimating the disease burden for different immunisation scenarios, but does not include the health impact assessment of excess COVID-19 disease burden attributable to these immunisation scenarios.
evidence: Statement about study limitations.

claim: Sustaining routine immunisation and resuming immunisation campaigns during the COVID-19 pandemic requires adaptations to service delivery with additional safety measures to protect health workers and the community from SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: While we have assessed the immunity gaps caused by immunisation service disruptions for measles, meningococcal A, and yellow fever vaccination in 10 low- and lower middle-income countries, sustaining routine immunisation and resuming immunisation campaigns during the COVID-19 pandemic requires adaptations to service delivery with additional safety measures to protect the health workers and the community from SARS-CoV-2 infection (Banks and Boonstoppel, 2020).
evidence: Statement about practical requirements for implementing vaccination during the pandemic, supported by citation.

claim: Infection prevention and control measures for vaccination during COVID-19 include personal protective equipment for health workers, children to be vaccinated, and their parents or caregivers.
source: Infection prevention and control measures include personal protective equipment for health workers, children to be vaccinated, and their parents or caregivers; additional prevention and control measures against SARS-CoV-2 infection at vaccination sites; physical distancing; and symptomatic screening and triaging (WHO, 2020e).
evidence: Description of recommended infection prevention measures, supported by WHO citation.

claim: COVID-19 transmission may be further mitigated by delivering several vaccines during a single campaign (such as measles and polio vaccines), or even combining vaccines with other age-relevant interventions such as nutritional supplements.
source: COVID-19 transmission may be further mitigated by delivering several vaccines during a single campaign (such as measles and polio vaccines), or even combining vaccines with other age-relevant interventions such as nutritional supplements.
evidence: Suggestion for how to reduce COVID-19 transmission risk during vaccination campaigns.

claim: Social mobilisation is needed to address the rumours, misinformation, and fear among the community to access vaccination safely during the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: Further, social mobilisation is needed to address the rumours, misinformation, and fear among the community to access vaccination safely during the COVID-19 pandemic (WHO, 2020g).
evidence: Statement about the need for social mobilisation, supported by WHO citation.

claim: The health impact assessment needs to be followed up by planning and implementation of catch-up vaccination to close the immunity gaps using a mixture of locally appropriate strategies to strengthen immunisation.
source: Therefore, our health impact assessment needs to be followed up by planning and implementation of catch-up vaccination to close the immunity gaps using a mixture of locally appropriate strategies to strengthen immunisation (Cutts et al., 2021), alongside access to additional operating costs to conduct routine and campaign immunisation services safely in COVID-secure environments while considering contextual factors and competing needs.
evidence: Recommendation for follow-up actions based on the study findings, supported by citation.
